newsitem.title: INDIA: India truck owners vow to continue strike.
newsitem.headline: India truck owners vow to continue strike.

text.p: India's truck owners on Wednesday vowed to continue their strike, which has kept two million vehicles off the road, until the government agreed to scrap a planned transport tax and rise in insurance premiums.

"They have come to a conclusion that unless the government drops service tax and the hefty hike in motor insurance premiums is re-examined by a transparent and independent tariff advisory committee, the strike will continue," S.P. Singh, a spokesman for the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
The truck owners met on Wednesday morning to discuss a government offer to break the deadlock and later held talks with the government.
"We had talks with the government and we understand they are trying to find a solution," Singh said.
"I am very optimistic. We had very positive talks with them in the past two days," Yogendra Narain, the highest ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters.
But the truckers showed no sign of relenting.

They launched the strike on Tuesday in protest against the service tax on the transport industry and a rise in insurance premiums. The protest has kept some 2.2 million trucks off the road and crippled ground transport of goods.

The AIMTC represents owners of about two million heavy trucks, one million light and medium-weight trucks and some 60,000 booking and delivery companies. Truckers move about 60 percent of India's goods.
The AIMTC objects to a five percent service tax on road transport which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed in the federal budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year.
It also opposes a decision by state-owned insurance companies which it said would raise insurance premiums by between 300 and 400 percent.
The government said on Tuesday that parliament would have to discuss the service tax proposals before they could take effect. It has also offered to put off the rise in insurance premiums.
Booking and delivery across the country have come to a standstill.
Trade groups have appealed to the truck owners to call off the strike in view of the current political crisis.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month-old minority government on Sunday lost the support of its key ally, the Congress party, and must face a vote of confidence by April 11. "It is not just commerce and industry, the common man will be severely affected if the strike continues," said a spokesman for a northern Indian trade chamber.
If it continues, the strike is expected to push up the prices of essential and perishable commodities.
